title: Position: Regulating Algorithms Is Not Enough. A Study of Content Discovery in Online Platforms
claim: Outcomes emerge from interactions among many interdependent components, so governing any single component in isolation is insufficient.
layout: 6 nodes in hexagon, fully connected by bidirectional arrows, callout definitions beside each
description: A hexagonal circuit diagram with six yellow rectangular nodes in bold uppercase condensed text: Engagements, Ripples (top row), Mediations, Experiences (middle row), Facilitators, Interpreters (bottom row). Gray double-headed arrows join every node to every other node, curving around the outside and crossing through the center in a dense web. Each node has an adjacent white box with a thin black border giving a one-sentence definition, for example 'Algorithmic and human curators which facilitate user discovery' or 'Mechanisms for interpreting, analyzing, and modeling a user's discovery objectives'. The background is white and the only strong color is yellow, so the eye lands on the node labels and then follows the crossing arrows. The all-to-all connectivity shows that no component operates independently.
caption: The Cultural Expressions Discovery Circuit, a cohesive framework for discovery within online platforms.
abstract: Recent AI regulation has largely focused on algorithmic components such as recommender models, ranking systems, and profiling mechanisms. At the same time, cultural and digital policy agendas increasingly frame discovery as a key objective, aiming to promote exposure diversity and cultural representation. We argue that these outcomes cannot be effectively governed through algorithm-centric approaches alone. Discovery does not arise from individual algorithms in isolation, but from interactions among models, interfaces, user behavior, economic incentives, and cultural norms. We introduce the Cultural Expressions Discovery Circuit (CEDC), an interdisciplinary framework that models discovery as an emergent socio-technical process. Through this lens, we illustrate how certain regulatory approaches struggle to align with broader cultural objectives. Furthermore, we highlight how socio-technical analysis can help inform both technical research and the governance of cultural expressions in online platforms.
